itens.nascimento: August 26, 1910, Skopje (then the Ottoman Empire, today North Macedonia)
fontes: Francis, Homily for the Canonization of Teresa of Calcutta (September 4, 2016)

itens.resumo: Polish religious sister of the twentieth century, a mystic of the Divine Mercy, whose revelations gave rise to the devotion and the liturgical feast bearing that name.
itens.corpo:
Helena Kowalska was born into a poor peasant family in central Poland and entered, as an adult, the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy, taking the name Faustina. She carried out humble tasks in the convents where she lived, as a cook, gardener and portress.

Throughout her religious life she reported numerous mystical experiences centered on the mercy of God, which she recorded out of obedience to her spiritual director in an extensive diary, published posthumously under the title "Diary: Divine Mercy in My Soul." From these experiences arose the devotion to the Divine Mercy, including the image of the Merciful Jesus and the prayer of the Chaplet of Divine Mercy.

She died of tuberculosis in Kraków in 1938, still little known outside her religious circle. Decades later, the then Archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła — the future Pope John Paul II — promoted the recognition of her writings and her cause for canonization. She was canonized in 2000, when John Paul II also instituted the Feast of Divine Mercy on the Second Sunday of Easter. Her liturgical memorial is celebrated on October 5.
fontes: John Paul II, Homily for the Canonization of Faustina Kowalska (April 30, 2000)
Saint Faustina Kowalska, Diary: Divine Mercy in My Soul

itens.resumo: Salvadoran archbishop assassinated in 1980 while celebrating Mass, for his defense of the poor and his denunciation of violence during the conflict in El Salvador.
itens.corpo:
Óscar Arnulfo Romero was born in Ciudad Barrios, El Salvador, and was ordained a priest in Rome. Initially regarded as a cleric with a moderate and cautious profile, he was appointed Archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, during a period of growing political violence and repression against peasants, catechists and priests committed to the defense of human rights.

The murder of a close friend, the Jesuit priest Rutilio Grande, a few weeks after Romero's installation, is often pointed to as a turning point in his pastoral work: Romero began to denounce publicly, in homilies broadcast by radio throughout the country, the violations committed by security forces and paramilitary groups, becoming a prominent voice in defense of the poor and of the victims of violence.

He was shot dead by a gunman while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel in San Salvador on March 24, 1980, a crime that remains associated with death squads linked to sectors of the Salvadoran far right. He was canonized in 2018, recognized by the Church as a martyr "in odium fidei" (in hatred of the faith). His feast is celebrated on March 24.
fontes: Francis, Homily for the Canonization of Óscar Romero (October 14, 2018)

itens.titulo: Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein)
itens.resumo: German Jewish philosopher who converted to Catholicism and became a Discalced Carmelite; she was killed in a gas chamber at Auschwitz. Co-patroness of Europe.
itens.corpo:
Edith Stein was born in Breslau, then in Germany (today Wrocław, in Poland), into a practicing Jewish family, and distinguished herself while still young as a philosopher, a student and assistant of the phenomenologist Edmund Husserl. She drifted away from the Jewish faith in adolescence, declaring herself an atheist for years, until a conversion marked, among other factors, by her reading of the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Avila, which led her to Catholic baptism in 1922.

In 1933, faced with the rise of Nazism and the first racial laws that barred her from teaching because of her Jewish origin, she entered the Carmel of Cologne, taking the name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Transferred to a convent in the Netherlands for safety, she was arrested in 1942 together with her sister Rosa, also a convert, as a reprisal by the Nazi regime for the protests of the Dutch Catholic bishops against the persecution of the Jews.

She died in a gas chamber at the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, probably on August 9, 1942. She was canonized in 1998 and, the following year, proclaimed co-patroness of Europe together with Bridget of Sweden and Catherine of Siena. Her feast is celebrated on August 9.
itens.nascimento: October 12, 1891, Breslau (then Germany, today Wrocław, Poland)
fontes: John Paul II, Homily for the Canonization of Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (October 11, 1998)
John Paul II, Apostolic Letter «Spes Aedificandi» (October 1, 1999)

itens.resumo: Belgian missionary who devoted sixteen years to the leper colony on the Hawaiian island of Molokai, himself contracting the disease.
itens.corpo:
Jozef de Veuster was born into a peasant family in Belgium and entered the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, taking the name Damien. Sent as a missionary to Hawaii in 1864, he was ordained a priest in Honolulu.

In 1873, he volunteered to serve in the compulsory isolation colony for people with Hansen's disease (leprosy) on the Kalaupapa peninsula, on the island of Molokai, which had by then been practically abandoned by the authorities. There he lived for nearly sixteen years, building houses, a water pipeline, a church, and coffins, organizing the daily life of the community and offering spiritual and material assistance to the sick, many of whom had been forcibly separated from their families.

He contracted the disease around 1884, and continued his work until his death in 1889. His dedication became an international symbol of heroic charity toward the outcast. He was canonized in 2009. His feast is celebrated on May 10.
fontes: Benedict XVI, Homily for the Canonization of Damien of Molokai (October 11, 2009)

itens.resumo: Italian pediatrician, wife and mother, who refused treatments that would have endangered the life of the child she was expecting, dying days after giving birth.
itens.corpo:
Gianna Beretta was born in Magenta, in northern Italy, and graduated in medicine, specializing in pediatrics. She practiced her profession with particular devotion to children, the elderly and the poorest, balancing her medical work with an intense life of faith and involvement in Catholic lay associations.

In 1955 she married the engineer Pietro Molla, with whom she had three children. During her fourth pregnancy, in 1961, she was diagnosed with a tumor in the uterus; she refused both abortion and the total hysterectomy that would have guaranteed her greater safety, choosing instead a procedure that would allow the pregnancy to continue its course, even though she was aware of the risks she was running.

Her daughter, Gianna Emanuela, was born healthy, but Gianna died of complications a week later, in 1962. She was canonized in 2004, with her husband and children present at the ceremony — a rare case in the history of the Church. She is venerated as patroness of mothers, physicians and the pro-life movement. Her feast is celebrated on April 28.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: AndyScott — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: John Paul II, Homily for the Canonization of Gianna Beretta Molla (May 16, 2004)

itens.resumo: Young Italian layman of the early twentieth century, engaged in works of charity and in Catholic Action, who died of fulminant poliomyelitis at the age of twenty-four.
itens.corpo:
Pier Giorgio Frassati was born in Turin, the son of Alfredo Frassati, founder and director of the newspaper La Stampa and an influential figure in Italian politics. Despite coming from a wealthy family that was not very observant, from adolescence he developed an intense spiritual life, marked by daily Eucharist, frequent confession and participation in Catholic movements such as Catholic Action and the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

He devoted much of his free time and of his own money to visiting and assisting poor families in the working-class neighborhoods of Turin, often hiding this activity even from his own family. He was also an enthusiastic mountaineer, and he organized mountain excursions with friends as an occasion for fellowship and spiritual deepening — a habit that, decades later, earned him a strong identification among young Catholics.

He died suddenly at the age of twenty-four, a victim of fulminant poliomyelitis, probably contracted through contact with the sick people he visited. Only after his death did his family discover the extent of his charitable activity, when they saw the funeral filled with poor people whom he had helped in secret. He was beatified in 1990 and canonized in 2025. He is the patron of young people, students and mountaineers; his feast is celebrated on July 4.
fontes: Leo XIV, Homily for the Canonization of Pier Giorgio Frassati and Carlo Acutis (September 7, 2025)
John Paul II, Homily for the Beatification of Pier Giorgio Frassati (May 20, 1990)

itens.resumo: Italian-British teenager of the early twenty-first century, devoted to the Eucharist and creator of a website on Eucharistic miracles; the first "millennial" saint of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Carlo Acutis was born in London to Italian parents and grew up in Milan. From childhood he showed an unusual devotion to the Eucharist, which he called his "highway to heaven", attending daily Mass and Eucharistic adoration as soon as he began to receive Holy Communion, having made his First Communion before the usual age.

Gifted with an early talent for computing, he used this knowledge in the service of the faith: he cataloged and documented dozens of Eucharistic miracles recognized by the Church around the world, gathering the material in a website that he put together while still a teenager and that remains available as a traveling exhibition in parishes in many countries. He also volunteered in charitable works with people experiencing homelessness and supported schoolmates who were victims of bullying.

He died at the age of fifteen, in 2006, of fulminant leukemia, facing the illness with a serenity that impressed his family and doctors. He was beatified in 2020 and canonized in 2025, becoming the first saint born in the millennial generation. He is popularly called the "patron of the internet". His feast is celebrated on October 12.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Esthappanos Bar Geevarghese — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: Leo XIV, Homily for the Canonization of Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati (September 7, 2025)

itens.resumo: A nineteenth-century French couple, parents of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux and of four other daughters who became religious; the first married couple canonized together by the Church.
itens.corpo:
Louis Martin, a watchmaker, and Zélie Guérin, a lacemaker specializing in the production of Alençon lace, married in 1858 in France and had nine children, of whom five daughters survived to adulthood — all of them became religious, among them Thérèse of Lisieux, future Doctor of the Church. The couple lived an intense Christian life, marked by daily Mass, family prayer, and charity to the poor, despite the common hardships of a large family of the time, including the early death of four of their children while still young.

Zélie also ran her own lace business, showing herself to be a woman of strong administrative ability as well as of intense spiritual life, recorded in a vast family correspondence now studied as a source on the Christian upbringing given to her daughters. She died of breast cancer in 1877, leaving Louis responsible for raising their still-young daughters, among them Thérèse, then four years old.

The couple's witness of Christian life, especially evidenced by Thérèse of Lisieux's later writings about her own childhood, became a reference of holiness lived in ordinary married and family life. They were canonized together in 2015, the first married couple to receive this honor in the same ceremony. Their joint liturgical memorial is celebrated on July 12.
itens.nascimento: Louis: August 22, 1823, Bordeaux (France); Zélie: December 23, 1831, Saint-Denis-sur-Sarthon (France)
itens.morte: Louis: July 29, 1894, Arnières-sur-Iton (France); Zélie: August 28, 1877, Alençon (France)
fontes: Francis, Homily for the Canonization of Louis and Zélie Martin (October 18, 2015)

itens.resumo: Apostle, called "brother of the Lord" (close relative), traditionally identified as the first bishop of Jerusalem.
itens.corpo: One of the Twelve, distinguished from James the Greater by the tradition that calls him "the Less" — whether by age or stature. Part of the tradition identifies him with the "James, the brother of the Lord" mentioned by Paul (Gal 1:19) and with the first bishop of the community of Jerusalem, presiding over the so-called "Council of Jerusalem" narrated in Acts 15. The Letter of James in the New Testament is traditionally attributed to him.

itens.resumo: One of the Twelve, presented in the Gospel of John as the disciple who brought Nathanael to Jesus.
itens.corpo: A native of Bethsaida, Philip appears in the Synoptic Gospels only in the lists of the Twelve, but the Gospel of John gives him a prominent role: it is he who calls Nathanael (Jn 1:43-46), he whom Jesus questions about how to feed the crowd (Jn 6:5-7), and he to whom pilgrim Greeks ask to see Jesus (Jn 12:20-22). Tradition places his preaching in Asia Minor, where he is said to have suffered martyrdom.

itens.resumo: One of the Twelve Apostles, identified in the Gospels by the epithet "the Zealot" or "the Cananean."
itens.corpo: Distinct from Simon Peter, this apostle receives in the Gospels the epithet "Zealot" (Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13), possibly linked to a Jewish group resisting the Roman occupation, or used in a more general sense of religious zeal. Scripture relates nothing more about him; later tradition associates him with a mission in Persia, alongside the apostle Jude Thaddeus.

itens.resumo: An Apostle distinct from Judas Iscariot, popularly invoked as the patron of difficult and impossible causes.
itens.corpo: Called "Thaddaeus" in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark to avoid confusion with Judas Iscariot, he is the traditional author of the brief Letter of Jude in the New Testament, which exhorts the faithful to persevere in the faith in the face of false teachers. Especially since the twentieth century, he has become one of the most widespread popular devotions in the Catholic world, invoked as an intercessor in situations considered humanly hopeless — hence his title "patron of impossible causes".

itens.resumo: Disciple chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot and complete the number of the Twelve.
itens.corpo: After the betrayal and death of Judas Iscariot, the Eleven gathered the community to choose a replacement from among those who had accompanied Jesus from the baptism of John until the Ascension. After praying, they cast lots between two candidates, and the lot fell on Matthias (Acts 1:15-26), who became part of the apostolic college before Pentecost. Tradition places his later preaching in the Caucasus or in Cappadocia.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Reinhardhauke — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

itens.resumo: A Levite disciple from Cyprus, Paul's companion on the first missionary journeys, called an "apostle" in an extended sense.
itens.corpo: Joseph, surnamed Barnabas ("son of encouragement") by the apostles, was a Levite native of Cyprus who sold his land for the benefit of the community in Jerusalem (Acts 4:36-37). It was he who introduced the newly converted Saul of Tarsus to the apostles, overcoming the community's initial distrust, and he accompanied him on the first missionary journey recounted in Acts. Although he was not one of the original Twelve, tradition attributes to him the title of apostle because of his foundational role in the mission to the Gentiles.

itens.resumo: Disciple and collaborator of Saint Paul, recipient of two pastoral letters of the New Testament.
itens.corpo: The son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, from Lystra, Timothy became one of Paul's closest collaborators, who calls him "beloved son" and entrusts to him the young community of Ephesus. The two Letters to Timothy, in the New Testament, deal with the organization of the communities and the formation of bishops and presbyters. Tradition identifies him as the first bishop of Ephesus.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: HVL — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

itens.resumo: A Greek disciple of Saint Paul, sent as a delegate to Corinth and later established in Crete.
itens.corpo: An uncircumcised Greek, Titus accompanied Paul to the so-called Council of Jerusalem as a test case on the non-obligatory nature of circumcision for Gentile converts (Gal 2:1-3). He served as Paul's emissary to the troubled community of Corinth and, according to the Letter to Titus, was left in Crete to organize that Church, appointing presbyters in the different cities of the island.

itens.resumo: Forerunner of Jesus, who baptized in the Jordan River and proclaimed the coming of the Messiah; beheaded by order of Herod Antipas.
itens.corpo: Son of Elizabeth and Zechariah, a relative of Mary, John devoted himself to an ascetic life in the desert of Judea and preached a baptism of repentance on the banks of the Jordan, where he also baptized Jesus. The Gospels present him as the one who prepared the way of the Messiah, fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah. He was beheaded by order of Herod Antipas, after publicly denouncing the latter's marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife. He is the only saint, besides Mary, whose birth the Church celebrates liturgically.

itens.resumo: A Galilean disciple healed by Jesus, present at the foot of the cross and the first witness of the Resurrection, called the "apostle to the apostles."
itens.corpo: A native of Magdala, in Galilee, Mary Magdalene is presented by the Gospels as a disciple who followed Jesus and supported him out of her own means, after having been freed from "seven demons" (Lk 8:2). She was among the women present at the crucifixion and at the empty tomb, and she was the first to whom the Risen One appeared (Jn 20:11-18), being sent to announce it to the apostles — which earned her, in tradition, the title "apostle to the apostles." In 2016, Pope Francis raised her liturgical memorial to the rank of feast, placing her liturgically on the same level as the apostles.

itens.resumo: Sister of Mary and Lazarus, hostess of Jesus in Bethany, who professes her faith before the raising of Lazarus.
itens.corpo: A resident of Bethany, near Jerusalem, Martha welcomed Jesus into her home (Lk 10:38-42) and is remembered for the episode in which she is busy with serving while her sister Mary listens to the Master. In the Gospel of John, it is she who professes to Jesus, before the raising of Lazarus, one of the most complete confessions of faith in the New Testament: "Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God" (Jn 11:27).

itens.resumo: Mother of Saint Augustine, whose prayers and tears over decades accompanied her son's conversion to Christianity.
itens.corpo: Born in Roman North Africa, Monica devoted more than fifteen years to praying for the conversion of her son Augustine, who was then living far from the Christian faith and from the moral teaching she had given him. She accompanied him to Rome and Milan, where she would live to see his conversion under the preaching of Saint Ambrose, an episode recounted by Augustine himself in the "Confessions". She died in Ostia, shortly afterward, on the way back to Africa. She is invoked as the patron saint of Christian mothers.

itens.resumo: Bishop of North Africa, one of the greatest theologians of the Christian West, author of the "Confessions" and "The City of God".
itens.corpo: Born in Tagaste (present-day Algeria) in 354, Augustine converted to Christianity in Milan in 386, under the influence of Saint Ambrose and the prayers of his mother, Saint Monica. Ordained bishop of Hippo, he produced an immense theological body of work — the "Confessions", "The City of God" and treatises against Donatism and Pelagianism — which decisively shaped Western theology on grace, original sin and the Church. He is venerated as a Doctor of the Church with the title "Doctor of Grace".

itens.resumo: Bishop of Milan in the fourth century, who baptized Saint Augustine and composed hymns that are still part of the Latin liturgy.
itens.corpo: A Roman official elected bishop of Milan by popular acclamation in 374, although still a catechumen, Ambrose became one of the great preachers and theologians of the West. He confronted Emperor Theodosius, imposing public penance on him for a massacre in Thessalonica, a famous episode concerning the limits of temporal power before the moral authority of the Church. He baptized Augustine at the Easter Vigil of 387. He is considered the father of Ambrosian chant and a Doctor of the Church.

itens.resumo: Monk and scholar of the 4th-5th century, translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) at the commission of Pope Damasus I.
itens.corpo: Born in Dalmatia, Jerome devoted a large part of his life to the study of the biblical languages, Hebrew and Greek, settled in Bethlehem, where he lived as a monk near the place of Christ's birth. His translation of the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate, became the official biblical text of the Latin Church for more than a thousand years. He is considered the greatest biblical exegete of Christian antiquity and a Doctor of the Church.

itens.resumo: Patriarch of Constantinople in the 4th-5th century, famed for his eloquence, which earned him the epithet "Chrysostom" ("golden mouth").
itens.corpo: A presbyter in Antioch before being elected Patriarch of Constantinople in 398, John became known for the exceptional quality of his homilies — many of which are still preserved — and for publicly denouncing the abuses of the imperial court, which cost him two exiles. He died in the second of them, in 407. He is a Doctor of the Church and the patron saint of preachers.

itens.resumo: Thirteenth-century Dominican friar, author of the "Summa Theologiae" and greatest exponent of Scholastic theology.
itens.corpo: Born near Aquino, in Italy, Thomas entered the newly founded Order of Preachers against the will of his noble family, who even kept him in captivity for more than a year to dissuade him. He studied with Albert the Great in Cologne and Paris and produced a monumental theological and philosophical synthesis, the "Summa Theologiae," which articulates the Christian faith with the philosophy of Aristotle. He is the Common Doctor of the Church, a central reference of Catholic philosophy and theology.

itens.resumo: Thirteenth-century Franciscan friar, minister general of the Order and mystical theologian, called the "Seraphic Doctor".
itens.corpo: Giovanni di Fidanza, who took the name Bonaventure upon entering the Order of Friars Minor, became its minister general in 1257, a period of crisis over the interpretation of the ideal of poverty left by Francis of Assisi. He wrote the official biography of Francis and works of mystical theology, such as the "Journey of the Mind to God". He took part in the Second Council of Lyon (1274), where he died. He is a Doctor of the Church.

itens.resumo: Fourteenth-century Dominican lay mystic who convinced Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome.
itens.corpo: A Dominican tertiary who never took formal monastic vows in the classical sense, Catherine of Siena lived an intense life of mysticism and charity in her native city in Tuscany, before becoming directly involved in the ecclesiastical politics of her time: she traveled to Avignon to persuade Pope Gregory XI to end the papal exile in France and return to Rome, which took place in 1377. Her work "The Dialogue of Divine Providence" is considered a classic of Italian mysticism. She was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1970 and co-patroness of Europe.

itens.resumo: Dominican friar of the 13th century, teacher of Thomas Aquinas, and a pioneer in the systematic study of the natural sciences within theology.
itens.corpo:
A Dominican bishop and theologian, Albert devoted himself to the study of practically all the knowledge available in his time — philosophy, theology, botany, mineralogy, astronomy —, seeking to reconcile Aristotelian reason with the Christian faith. He was a professor of Thomas Aquinas in Cologne and Paris, publicly acknowledging the talent of his then young and reserved disciple. He is the patron saint of natural scientists and a Doctor of the Church.

Born in Germany at the beginning of the 13th century, he left as a young man for Padua, where he studied the liberal arts and showed the interest in the natural sciences that would mark his life. There he attended the Dominican church and, after overcoming doubts and resistance from his family, entered the Order, receiving the habit from the hands of Blessed Jordan of Saxony. Ordained a priest, he taught at several centers of study and furthered his own training in Paris.

In 1248 he was given the task of opening a center of theological studies in Cologne, taking Thomas Aquinas with him, and a relationship of esteem and friendship was born between the two. In 1254 he was elected provincial of the Dominicans of a vast territory of Central and Northern Europe, which he visited in person. Pope Alexander IV wanted him at his side as a theological consultant and appointed him bishop of Regensburg, a diocese in a difficult moment, which he governed from 1260 to 1262, bringing peace to the city, reorganizing parishes and convents, and promoting works of charity.

In 1263 and 1264 he preached in Germany and Bohemia at the commission of Urban IV, afterward returning to Cologne to teach and write. His authority made him a man of reconciliation, as in the dispute between the Archbishop of Cologne and the municipal institutions. The title "Great," Benedict XVI recalls, indicates the vastness of his doctrine joined to holiness of life.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of March 24, 2010 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Portuguese Franciscan friar of the thirteenth century, renowned preacher and Doctor of the Church, popularly invoked to find lost objects.
itens.corpo:
Fernando de Bulhões, born in Lisbon, first entered the Augustinian canons and later changed orders, becoming a Franciscan friar with the name Anthony, drawn by the example of the first Franciscan martyrs of Morocco. He became one of the greatest preachers of his time in northern Italy, especially in Padua, where he died in 1231. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1946. Popular devotion invokes him to find lost objects, a tradition linked to an episode concerning a psalter that had been taken from him.

Born in Lisbon around 1195, into a noble family, and baptized Fernando, he entered the canons who followed the Rule of Saint Augustine, first at Saint Vincent in Lisbon and then at Santa Cruz in Coimbra, where he studied the Bible and the Fathers of the Church. It was in Coimbra that, in 1220, he saw the relics of the first five Franciscan missionaries martyred in Morocco, an event that led him to ask to become a Friar Minor.

He took the name Anthony and set out for Morocco, but an illness forced him to go to Italy. In 1221 he attended the Chapter of Mats in Assisi, where he met Saint Francis. He lived hidden in a hermitage in Forlì until he preached, by chance, at a priestly ordination, when his learning and eloquence were revealed. He then preached in Italy and France and was one of the first teachers of theology among the Friars Minor, if not the first: he taught in Bologna with the blessing of Saint Francis, who wrote to him: "It pleases me that you teach sacred theology to the brothers".

He died at the gates of Padua on June 13, 1231, and Gregory IX, who had called him the Ark of the Testament, canonized him a year later, in 1232. At the end of his life he wrote the Sunday Sermons and the Sermons on the Saints, intended for preachers and teachers of his Order.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of February 10, 2010 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Sixteenth-century Spanish Carmelite friar, co-founder of the Discalced Carmelites with Teresa of Ávila and master of the mysticism of the "dark night."
itens.corpo: Juan de Yepes joined Teresa of Ávila in the reform of Carmel, founding the male branch of the Discalced. He was even imprisoned and mistreated by Carmelite friars opposed to the reform, a period in which he composed part of his mystical poetry. His works — "Dark Night," "Spiritual Canticle" and "Living Flame of Love" — describe the soul's path of purification toward union with God. He is a Doctor of the Church with the title "Mystical Doctor."

itens.resumo: Bishop of Geneva in the 17th century, author of the "Introduction to the Devout Life" and Doctor of the Church, patron of journalists and writers.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Geneva in a context of strong Calvinist presence, Francis de Sales devoted himself to persuasive and gentle preaching, summed up in his best-known work, "Introduction to the Devout Life" (1609), addressed to laypeople seeking holiness in the midst of ordinary life. Together with Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, he founded the Order of the Visitation. He is a Doctor of the Church and, since 1923, patron of Catholic journalists and writers.

itens.resumo: Neapolitan bishop of the 18th century, founder of the Redemptorists and Doctor of the Church in moral theology.
itens.corpo:
A Neapolitan lawyer who abandoned his legal career, Alphonsus became a priest and founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer (Redemptorists), dedicated to popular evangelization in the poorest rural areas of the Kingdom of Naples. He wrote extensively on moral theology, defending a middle path between rigorism and laxism — the so-called "equiprobabilism". He is a Doctor of the Church and patron of confessors and moralists.

Born in 1696 into a noble family of Naples, he earned a degree in civil and canon law at the age of 16 and, for eight years, won every case he argued. In 1723, indignant at the corruption and injustice of the courts, he left the profession and decided to become a priest, against his father's wishes. He was ordained in 1726 and began evangelizing the humblest classes of Naples.

From this preaching arose the so-called evening chapels: groups that gathered at night in homes and workshops to pray and meditate on the Word of God, guided by catechists trained by him. According to Benedict XVI, they were a source of moral education and mutual help among the poor, to the point that theft, duels and prostitution almost disappeared. At the age of 35, moved by the religious neglect of the peasants and shepherds of the countryside, he left the capital and, in 1732, founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, whose itinerant missionaries reached the most remote villages.

Appointed bishop of Sant'Agata de' Goti in 1762, he left the post in 1775 because of illness. He died in 1787 and, on hearing the news, Pius VI exclaimed: "He was a saint!". He was canonized in 1839 and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1871. He is also the author of the lyrics and music of Tu scendi dalle stelle, one of the most popular Christmas carols in Italy.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of March 30, 2011 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Jesuit and cardinal of the 16th-17th century, theologian of the Counter-Reformation and Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo:
An Italian Jesuit of great theological formation, Bellarmine became one of the principal defenders of Catholic doctrine in the face of the Protestant controversy, systematized in his work "Disputationes de Controversiis". As a consultant to the Holy Office, he was involved in the initial proceedings against Galileo Galilei, adopting at the time a relatively moderate stance within the context of the controversy. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Born on October 4, 1542 in Montepulciano, near Siena, and a nephew of Pope Marcellus II on his mother's side, he entered the Society of Jesus on September 20, 1560. He studied philosophy and theology at the Roman College, in Padua and in Louvain, drawing on Saint Thomas and the Fathers of the Church. He was ordained a priest on March 25, 1570 and taught theology in Louvain before being called to Rome.

At the Roman College, he held the chair of Apologetics from 1576 to 1586, and from these lectures the Controversies were born, written shortly after the Council of Trent, when the Church needed to reaffirm its identity in the face of the Reformation. Benedict XVI points to them as a reference still valid for Catholic ecclesiology: they deal with Revelation, the nature of the Church, the sacraments, and theological anthropology, presenting doctrine with reason and Tradition, without a polemical tone. Between 1588 and 1594 he was spiritual father to the Jesuit students, among them Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. From 1597 to 1598 comes his most popular work, the catechism Christian Doctrine in Brief.

Clement VIII appointed him papal theologian and created him a cardinal on March 3, 1599. Archbishop of Capua from 1602, he visited the parishes every week and promoted three diocesan synods and one provincial council. He returned to Rome to serve in several congregations of the Holy See and, in his last years, wrote books on spirituality. He died in Rome on September 17, 1621. Pius XI beatified him in 1923, canonized him in 1930, and proclaimed him a Doctor of the Church in 1931.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of February 23, 2011 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Sixteenth-century Dutch Jesuit, author of catechisms widely used during the Counter-Reformation in central Europe.
itens.corpo:
One of the first Jesuits north of the Alps, Canisius devoted himself to consolidating Catholicism in Germany, Austria and Bohemia during a period of strong Protestant advance, founding colleges and writing catechisms — the "Large Catechism" and the "Small Catechism" — which went through hundreds of editions and shaped generations of German-speaking Catholics. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Peter Kanis, Canisius in its Latinized form, was born in Nijmegen, in the Netherlands, on May 8, 1521, the son of the city's burgomaster. A student in Cologne, he entered the Society of Jesus on May 8, 1543, in Mainz, after making the Spiritual Exercises under Peter Faber, one of the first companions of Saint Ignatius. Ordained in 1546, the following year he was at the Council of Trent as a theologian of the Bishop of Augsburg. Saint Ignatius assigned him to the apostolate in Germany, a mission he received while praying in Saint Peter's Basilica in 1549.

In Bavaria, he was dean, rector and vice-chancellor of the University of Ingolstadt. In Vienna, where he administered the diocese for a brief period, he served in hospitals and prisons and prepared his catechism. He founded the College of Prague in 1556 and until 1569 was the first superior of the Jesuit province of Upper Germany, creating the network of colleges that Benedict XVI points to as the starting point of Catholic renewal in those countries. He took part in the Colloquy of Worms with Melanchthon (1557), was nuncio in Poland (1558) and returned to Trent for the final session of the Council, in 1562.

In 1580 he retired to Fribourg, in Switzerland, devoting himself to preaching and writing, and there he died on December 21, 1597. He was beatified by Pius IX in 1864, called the second Apostle of Germany by Leo XIII in 1897, and canonized and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1925.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of February 9, 2011 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: English Benedictine monk of the 8th century, author of the "Ecclesiastical History of the English People" and Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo: A monk of the monastery of Jarrow, in northern England, Bede devoted his life to study and teaching, producing biblical commentaries, works on chronology — he was one of the first to date events systematically by the Christian era (B.C./A.D.) — and his masterpiece, the "Ecclesiastical History of the English People", the main source on the Christianization of Anglo-Saxon England. He is the only native English author among the Doctors of the Church.

itens.resumo: German Benedictine abbess of the twelfth century, mystic, composer, and author of treatises on natural medicine; Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo: Abbess of the monastery of Rupertsberg, in the Rhine valley, Hildegard combined mystical visions—recorded in her work "Scivias"—with a remarkably diverse output: musical compositions that survive to this day, treatises on medicinal plants and human physiology, and correspondence with popes and emperors. She was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Cappadocia in the 4th century, organizer of Eastern monasticism and Doctor of the Church, one of the three "Cappadocian Fathers."
itens.corpo: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Basil wrote monastic rules that became the foundation of Eastern monasticism to this day, founded institutions to assist the poor and the sick, and defended the Nicene doctrine on the divinity of the Holy Spirit in the face of Arianism, then dominant at the imperial court. Together with his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory Nazianzen, he forms the group of the "Cappadocian Fathers." He is a Doctor of the Church.

itens.resumo: Patriarch of Constantinople and theologian of the fourth century, called "the Theologian" by the Eastern tradition; Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo: A friend of Basil the Great since their studies in Athens, Gregory presided over the First Council of Constantinople (381), which reaffirmed and completed the Nicene Creed. He is one of the very rare Christian authors to whom the Byzantine tradition reserves the title "the Theologian" (together with John the Evangelist), because of his orations on the Trinity. He is a Doctor of the Church.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Alexandria in the fourth century, the foremost defender of the divinity of Christ against Arianism at the Council of Nicaea.
itens.corpo: While still a deacon, Athanasius accompanied his bishop to the Council of Nicaea (325) and, in the following decades as bishop, became the firmest opponent of Arianism, a doctrine that denied the full divinity of the Son. His resistance cost him five exiles over the course of his life, under different emperors. He is a Doctor of the Church and the author of the most influential ancient monastic biography, the "Life of Saint Anthony".

itens.resumo: Gallic bishop of the fourth century, called the "Athanasius of the West" for his defense of the Nicene faith against Arianism.
itens.corpo:
Bishop of Poitiers, in Gaul, Hilary converted to Christianity as an adult, coming from a pagan philosophical formation, and became one of the main Western defenders of the faith defined at Nicaea, which earned him exile imposed by the Arian emperor Constantius II. He wrote the treatise "On the Trinity", a landmark of ancient Latin Trinitarian theology. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Certain information about a good part of his life is lacking. Ancient sources say he was born in Poitiers, probably around 310, into a wealthy family and with a solid literary education, and that he came to the faith through a personal path of searching for the truth. Baptized around 345, he was elected bishop of his native city around 353 or 354. His first work, the Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, is the oldest Latin commentary on that Gospel to have come down to us.

In 356, at the Synod of Béziers, dominated by bishops favorable to Arianism and which he called the synod of the false apostles, his adversaries asked the emperor to exile him. In Phrygia, in present-day Turkey, he worked for the unity of the Church on the basis of the faith of Nicaea and began the treatise On the Trinity, starting from the formula of Baptism to show that the Father and the Son are of the same substance. He also wrote the Book of Synods to inform the bishops of Gaul.

Firm against the radical Arians, he was conciliatory toward those who admitted only that the Son was similar to the Father, seeking to bring them to the full faith. Benedict XVI sees in this his gift: uniting strength in the faith with gentleness in dealing with others. He returned to Poitiers in 360 or 361, and ancient authors attribute to him in large part the anti-Arian change in the episcopate of Gaul.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of October 10, 2007 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: A soldier and martyr of the early centuries of Christianity, whose legend of the fight against the dragon became a symbol of victory over evil.
itens.corpo: Historical documentation about George is scarce: tradition places him as a Roman soldier martyred under the Emperor Diocletian, in the early fourth century, probably in Palestine. The famous medieval account of the fight against a dragon to save a princess is a later hagiographic legend, with no historical claim, but it consolidated his cult as a Christian symbol of the victory of good over evil. He is the patron saint of England and Georgia, and is the object of intense popular devotion in Brazil.

itens.resumo: A martyr of the early centuries, traditional patron saint of travelers, who according to legend crossed a river carrying the Child Jesus.
itens.corpo: Little is known historically about Christopher, whose veneration goes back at least to the fifth century in the East. The hagiographical tradition relates that, being a man of great stature, he devoted himself to carrying travelers across a dangerous river, and once he carried a child of supernaturally increasing weight, who turned out to be Christ himself — an episode that gave rise to his name, "Christophoros" ("Christ-bearer"), and to the devotion to him as patron of travelers and drivers.

itens.resumo: Virgin and martyr of Sicily in the early fourth century, traditionally invoked as protector of sight.
itens.corpo: A young woman of Syracuse, in Sicily, Lucy consecrated herself to God and distributed her possessions to the poor, refusing an arranged marriage — a decision that, according to tradition, led her suitor to denounce her to the authorities during the persecution of Diocletian. She died a martyr around 304. Her name, linked to the Latin word for "light," consolidated the popular devotion that invokes her as protector of sight.

itens.resumo: Bishop and physician of Armenia, martyr of the early fourth century, invoked against throat ailments.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Sebaste, in Armenia, and trained in medicine, Blaise is said to have lived as a hermit in a cave during a persecution, also caring for wild animals that sought him out. Arrested and martyred, he is remembered for a traditional episode in which he is said to have saved a child who was choking on a fish bone — the origin of the blessing of throats carried out on his feast day in many parishes.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Giovanni Dall'Orto — Wikimedia Commons, Attribution

itens.resumo: Priest and martyr of the third century, whose veneration gave rise, in Western popular tradition, to the association with Valentine's Day.
itens.corpo: The historical documentation about Valentine is fragmentary, possibly merging accounts of more than one martyr of the same name in third-century Rome. The popular association with romantic love took hold mainly from the English Middle Ages onward, without a clear basis in ancient hagiography. The Church keeps his memorial as optional, focusing above all on his witness of faith, distinct from the commercial meaning the date later acquired.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Asia Minor in the 4th century, famous for his charity to the poor; the historical origin of the figure of Santa Claus.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Myra, in present-day Turkey, Nicholas is remembered through traditional accounts of discreet generosity, among them that of having secretly given gold to keep three young women from being sold into slavery for lack of a dowry — an episode at the origin of the custom of giving gifts in his name. His devotion, intense in both the East and the medieval West, gave rise, through later cultural paths in the Netherlands and the United States, to the popular figure of Santa Claus ("Santa Claus", from "Sinterklaas").

itens.resumo: Fifth-century missionary, apostle and patron saint of Ireland, who evangelized the island after having been enslaved there in his youth.
itens.corpo: Born in Roman Britain, Patrick was kidnapped by Irish pirates as a teenager and enslaved in Ireland for six years, a period during which he deepened his faith. He escaped, became a priest and later a bishop, and returned to Ireland as a missionary, devoting decades to the evangelization of the island, then predominantly pagan. He is the patron saint of Ireland, and his feast is celebrated by Irish communities throughout the world.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Nheyob — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.resumo: Eighth-century English monk, called the "Apostle of Germany" for his evangelization of the Germanic peoples.
itens.corpo:
An English Benedictine missionary, Boniface devoted decades to the evangelization of the Germanic peoples, reorganizing the ecclesiastical structure of the region under the mandate of Popes Gregory II and Gregory III. He is remembered for the episode in which he felled the "Oak of Thor," a pagan sacred tree, without suffering the divine punishment the locals expected — a gesture said to have prompted numerous conversions. He died a martyr in Frisia, already in his eighties, in 754.

He was born in Wessex, to an Anglo-Saxon family, around 675, and was baptized Winfrid. He entered the monastery at a very young age, taught Latin grammar, and wrote treatises and poetry. Ordained around the age of thirty, he felt called to evangelize the pagans of the continent. His first attempt, in Frisia, in 716, failed in the face of opposition from the local chief.

Two years later he went to Rome, where Pope Gregory II gave him the name Boniface and, with official letters, the mission to preach in Germania. The same pope consecrated him a bishop. Gregory III appointed him archbishop of all the Germanic tribes, with the authority to organize the ecclesiastical hierarchy there, and Pope Zachary confirmed his office. Benedict XVI emphasizes how much he prized communion with the Roman Pontiff.

Besides founding dioceses and holding synods, he promoted the creation of monasteries for men and women, calling Benedictine monks and nuns from his homeland to help proclaim the Gospel and spread the sciences and the arts. For him, working for the Gospel was also working for a true human culture.
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience of March 11, 2009 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Greek missionary brothers of the 9th century, "Apostles of the Slavs," creators of the alphabet that gave rise to the Cyrillic script.
itens.corpo: Byzantine brothers from Thessalonica, Cyril and Methodius were sent as missionaries to Great Moravia, where they translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into Old Church Slavonic, creating for this purpose an alphabet of their own — the Glagolitic, the basis of the later Cyrillic alphabet. They defended the liturgical use of the Slavic vernacular languages in the face of resistance, obtaining papal approval. They are co-patrons of Europe, alongside Benedict of Nursia.

itens.resumo: Spanish peasant of the 11th-12th century, patron saint of farmers and rural workers.
itens.corpo: A humble farmer from Madrid, Isidore is remembered for his simple life of work in the fields united with deep piety and charity toward the poorest. Tradition attributes to him several accounts of miraculous intervention on behalf of the needy. He became one of the most venerated popular saints in the rural world of the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Joseolgon — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

itens.resumo: Duke of Bohemia in the 10th century, martyr and patron saint of the Czech Republic, celebrated in the Christmas carol "Good King Wenceslas."
itens.corpo: A Christian duke of Bohemia, Wenceslaus promoted the evangelization of his duchy and maintained peaceful relations with the Kingdom of Germany, a policy that generated internal opposition. He was murdered by his own brother, Boleslaus, in 935, and quickly came to be venerated as a martyr and national patron saint. His memory inspired the well-known English-language Christmas carol "Good King Wenceslas."
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Michal Maňas — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

itens.resumo: King of France in the thirteenth century, known for his justice, his charity and his participation in the Crusades.
itens.corpo: King of France from 1226 to 1270, Louis IX is remembered for his just administration of the kingdom, for founding hospitals and for his personal practice of charity toward the poor, whom he received and served at his own table. He took part in two crusades, to the East and to North Africa, dying of plague during the second, near Tunis. He is a Catholic model of the Christian ruler and the patron of Franciscan tertiaries.

itens.resumo: A thirteenth-century Hungarian princess who, widowed while still young, dedicated her life and fortune to the care of the poor and the sick.
itens.corpo: The daughter of the King of Hungary, married at the age of fourteen to the Landgrave of Thuringia, Elizabeth was widowed at twenty, when her husband died on his way to a crusade. Driven from the court by her late husband's relatives, she devoted the rest of her brief life — she died at the age of 24 — to caring for the sick and the poor, becoming a Franciscan tertiary. She is the patroness of Catholic charitable works.

itens.resumo: The first person born in the United States to be canonized; foundress of the American Sisters of Charity and pioneer of the Catholic parochial school in the country.
itens.corpo: Born in New York into an Episcopalian family, Elizabeth Ann Bayley Seton converted to Catholicism after being widowed, a decision that cost her the estrangement of part of her family and friends. In Maryland she founded the first women's religious congregation of American origin, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph, and the first free Catholic parochial school in the United States. She was canonized by Paul VI in 1975, the first person born in the country to receive this recognition.

itens.resumo: The Curé of Ars, a nineteenth-century French parish priest known for his long hours in the confessional; patron saint of parish priests.
itens.corpo: Struggling in his studies, especially in Latin, John Mary Vianney almost was not ordained a priest, but he later devoted himself, in the small parish of Ars, to an intense ministry of confession, spending as many as sixteen hours a day in the confessional in the last years of his life, drawing pilgrims from all over France. He is the patron saint of parish priests and of diocesan clergy.

itens.resumo: A young French peasant girl who reported the Marian apparitions at Lourdes in 1858 and later became a religious sister.
itens.corpo:
The daughter of a very poor family of Lourdes, Bernadette reported, at the age of fourteen, eighteen apparitions of a "Lady" at the grotto of Massabielle, which the Church has recognized as the apparition of Our Lady of Lourdes. She endured skepticism and interrogations by civil and ecclesiastical authorities, always maintaining the same simple account. She became a religious of the Sisters of Charity of Nevers, where she died in 1879, and was canonized in 1933.

Her body was exhumed three times (1909, 1919 and 1925) for the beatification process and found to be surprisingly well preserved — hands and nails intact, according to the physicians present. Today it rests in a glass reliquary in the chapel of the convent of Saint-Gildard, in Nevers: thin wax masks have covered the face and hands since 1925, made to disguise the natural darkening of the skin in contact with the air — the Church has never officially stated that this is a supernatural state.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Roock, retouched by Rabanus Flavus — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

itens.resumo: Nineteenth-century French religious sister to whom, according to tradition, Our Lady revealed the design of the Miraculous Medal.
itens.corpo: A Daughter of Charity in Paris, Catherine Labouré reported, in 1830, apparitions of Our Lady who, it is said, showed her the design of a medal bearing the invocation "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee" — the origin of the devotion to the Miraculous Medal, first struck in 1832 and distributed since then in hundreds of millions of copies. She kept the apparitions secret for decades, revealing them only to her confessor.

itens.titulo: Saint Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort
itens.resumo: French missionary of the 17th-18th century, author of "True Devotion to Mary," influential in Marian spirituality.
itens.corpo: A missionary priest in rural France, Montfort preached popular missions and founded religious congregations — the Company of Mary (Montfort Missionaries) and the Daughters of Wisdom. His work "True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin," rediscovered and published only in the 19th century, had great influence on modern Marian spirituality, among others on John Paul II, whose papal motto "Totus Tuus" comes from this tradition.

itens.resumo: A fifteenth-century French peasant girl who led troops in the Hundred Years' War, guided by heavenly voices, and was burned as a heretic before being rehabilitated.
itens.corpo: A young peasant girl from Domrémy, Joan claimed to have received, from adolescence, messages from saints urging her to come to the aid of the King of France in the Hundred Years' War. She led French troops to decisive victories, among them the siege of Orléans (1429), but was captured by allies of the English, tried by an ecclesiastical court favorable to them, and burned as a heretic in 1431, at the age of nineteen. A new trial, ordered by Pope Callixtus III in 1456, annulled the condemnation; she was canonized in 1920.

itens.resumo: Italian Franciscan friar of the 17th century, associated in the hagiographic tradition with episodes of ecstasy and levitation.
itens.corpo: A Conventual friar of humble origins and little formal education, Joseph became known for a life of intense Eucharistic devotion, with which numerous accounts by witnesses of the time associated extraordinary phenomena of ecstasy. By popular association with these narratives, he is invoked as patron of students and aviators.

itens.resumo: Fifteenth-century Italian hermit, founder of the Order of Minims, known for his extreme austerity and as an adviser to kings.
itens.corpo: Hermit of Calabria who founded the Order of Minim Friars — the name expresses the desire to be considered the least among religious —, marked by perpetual fasting and radical austerity. He was summoned to the French court by Louis XI, who sought his intercession against imminent death, and he remained in France in the spiritual service of the crown until the end of his life. He is patron saint of sailors and boatmen of southern Italy.

itens.resumo: Roman priest of the sixteenth century, founder of the Oratory, known for his good humor and for his informal evangelization of the young people of Rome.
itens.corpo: Called "the saint of joy," Philip Neri devoted himself in Rome to the evangelization of young people and ordinary folk through informal methods—conversations, music, excursions—gathering around him the group that would give rise to the Congregation of the Oratory. He repeatedly refused promotion to the cardinalate, preferring direct contact with the simple people of Rome.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Didier Descouens — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.resumo: Italian priest of the 16th century, co-founder of the Theatines, invoked as patron saint of the unemployed.
itens.corpo: A lawyer who became a priest, Cajetan co-founded in Rome the Congregation of Clerics Regular (Theatines), devoted to the reform of the clergy and to assisting the poor and the sick in times of plague and famine. He is popularly invoked, especially in Brazil, as patron of employment and of material providence.

itens.resumo: Spanish Dominican friar of the 14th-15th century, an itinerant preacher who traveled throughout Europe calling for conversion and peace during the Western Schism.
itens.corpo: A Dominican from Valencia of great fame as a preacher, Vincent Ferrer traveled on foot through much of western Europe for decades, preaching penance amid the climate of uncertainty of the Great Western Schism. He contributed to the end of the schism by withdrawing, in 1416, the support he had given to one of the rival claimants to the papacy.

itens.resumo: Italian Franciscan friar of the fifteenth century, a renowned preacher devoted to the name of Jesus (the IHS monogram).
itens.corpo: A Franciscan of the Observance, Bernardine devoted himself to popular preaching throughout Italy, promoting devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, symbolized in the "IHS" monogram that he spread on tablets displayed in the cities — a gesture that also gave rise, at first, to suspicions of heterodoxy, of which he was cleared by the Holy See.

itens.resumo: French pilgrim of the 14th century, traditionally invoked against epidemics and plagues.
itens.corpo: According to tradition, Roch, born into a noble family of Montpellier, distributed his goods and went on pilgrimage to Rome, devoting himself to caring for victims of the plague in several Italian cities, until he himself contracted the disease. He is one of the saints most invoked against epidemics in European popular tradition, together with Saint Sebastian.

itens.resumo: A martyr of uncertain date and origin, whose veneration is widely spread, popularly invoked for urgent causes.
itens.corpo: Historical information about Expeditus is extremely scarce, and his historical existence is debated by historians; popular devotion, however, spread widely from the nineteenth century onward, above all because of a popular etymology that associates his name with the idea of speed, establishing his cult as that of an intercessor for urgent causes.

itens.resumo: Twin brothers, physicians and martyrs of the early centuries, patrons of physicians and pharmacists, with strong popular devotion in Brazil.
itens.corpo: According to tradition, Cosmas and Damian were twin brothers and physicians in the region of Cilicia or Syria, who treated the sick free of charge — hence the Greek epithet "anargyroi", "without silver" — before being martyred under Roman persecution at the beginning of the fourth century. They are patrons of physicians and pharmacists, with popular devotion especially intense in Brazil, where it is traditional to hand out sweets on their feast day.

itens.resumo: Young Italian mystic of the late 19th century, associated with mystical phenomena such as the stigmata, who died at the age of 25.
itens.corpo: A young lay woman from Lucca, in Tuscany, Gemma Galgani lived only 25 years, marked by severe physical illness and, according to accounts from her diary and her confessor, extraordinary mystical phenomena, among them the stigmata of the Passion. She desired to become a Passionist nun, but her frail health prevented her formal entrance into the order.

itens.resumo: Young Italian girl of the early twentieth century, killed at the age of eleven while resisting a sexual assault; she forgave her attacker before dying.
itens.corpo: The daughter of a very poor peasant family near Rome, Maria Goretti was attacked by a neighbor who tried to rape her; she resisted and was stabbed, dying the following day, in 1902, at the age of eleven, after declaring that she forgave her attacker. He, Alessandro Serenelli, was converted years later in prison and even took part in the ceremony of Maria's canonization, in 1950, present among the crowd.

itens.resumo: A young Italian nobleman who renounced his inheritance, entered the Society of Jesus, and died caring for the sick during an epidemic in Rome.
itens.corpo:
Aloysius Gonzaga was born on March 9, 1568, in Castiglione delle Stiviere, in northern Italy, the firstborn of a noble family. His father expected him to inherit the marquisate and pursue a military career, but from an early age Aloysius developed an intense life of prayer and asceticism. After receiving his First Communion from the hands of Saint Charles Borromeo, he became interested in the mission of the Jesuits and began teaching catechism.

In 1585 he formally renounced his rights of inheritance and entered the Society of Jesus, in Rome, on November 25 of the same year. He took his religious vows in 1587 and began his studies in theology. During the epidemic that struck Rome in 1591, he volunteered to serve the sick in the Jesuit hospital. While transporting and caring for the ill, he contracted a disease that left him gravely weakened.

Aloysius died in Rome on June 21, 1591, at the age of 23. He was beatified by Paul V in 1605 and canonized by Benedict XIII on December 31, 1726. In 1729, Benedict XIII declared him patron of youth and of students; Pius XI extended this patronage to all Christian youth. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on June 21.

itens.resumo: Young Polish Jesuit who left Vienna on foot, reached Rome in 1567, and died in the novitiate at the age of eighteen.
itens.corpo:
Stanislaus Kostka was born in Rostkowo, Poland, in 1550, into a noble family. In 1564 he was sent to Vienna to study at the Jesuit college with his older brother, Paul. During his years of study, his desire to enter the Society of Jesus grew, but he met with opposition from his family and hesitation from the local superiors, who feared conflict with his father.

In August 1567, he left Vienna disguised in humble clothes and began the journey on foot. He passed through Dillingen, where his vocation was examined by Saint Peter Canisius, and continued to Rome with other Jesuits. He arrived on October 25, 1567, and was received into the novitiate of Saint Andrew, under the direction of the Society of Jesus.

The novitiate lasted less than a year. After falling ill in early August 1568, Stanislaus died in Rome during the night of August 14 to 15, the solemnity of the Assumption of Our Lady. Pope Francis recalled his journey from Rostkowo to Vienna and Rome as a path toward holiness and presented to young people his motto: “Ad maiora natus sum,” “I was born for greater things.” He was beatified in 1605 and canonized on December 31, 1726. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on November 13.
fontes: Pope Francis, Message for the 450th Anniversary of the Death of Saint Stanislaus Kostka, Aug. 15, 2018 (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Servite friar from Forlì (c. 1265-1345), converted after assaulting Saint Philip Benizi; cured of a cancer in his leg on the eve of its amputation and invoked as patron of cancer patients.
itens.corpo:
Peregrine Laziosi was born in Forlì, in Romagna, around 1265, into a noble family. In his youth, according to tradition, he was active among the Ghibellines — the party allied with the emperor and opposed to the papacy — and had a reputation for a violent temper, to the point of being nicknamed "the hurricane." Around 1281, when the prior general of the Servants of Mary, Philip Benizi, went to Forlì to preach reconciliation with the pope, Peregrine was part of the group that drove him out of the city and attacked him with punches and slaps. Philip Benizi, without retaliating, offered the other cheek; touched by this evangelical response, the young man repented, sought forgiveness, and changed his life radically.

Near the age of thirty, Peregrine entered the Order of the Servants of Mary, founded shortly before in Florence and officially approved in 1304, making his novitiate in the convent of Siena. Back in Forlì, he spent the rest of his life in prayer, manual labor, and visiting the poor and sick of the city and the countryside, caring above all for the dying. Tradition describes two penances that marked his body: never sitting when he could stand, and keeping a strict silence. According to the most widespread version, it was this practice of remaining on his feet for long years — some say for thirty — that caused him varicose veins which degenerated into a malignant sore on his right leg.

In old age, he was struck by a tumor that was corroding the bone, and the physicians prepared to amputate his foot to save his life. On the eve of the operation, Peregrine dragged himself to the prayer room, prostrated himself before a crucifix, and begged for healing; he fell asleep there and, according to the account, had a vision of Jesus coming down from the cross to touch his leg. The next morning, the physician found the leg completely healed. This episode, recounted in the hagiographical sources and spread through popular devotion, is the reason he is invoked as a protector against cancer. He died in the Servite convent of Forlì on May 1, 1345, at about eighty years of age; his body is venerated in the basilica that bears his name in the city, where it is displayed incorrupt.

Peregrine was beatified by Clement XI on September 11, 1702, and canonized by Benedict XIII on December 27, 1726. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on May 1, the day of his death, although some calendars and dioceses keep it on May 4. He is patron of Forlì and of those suffering from cancer and prolonged illnesses, and those living with incurable diseases also turn to him. His connection with Saint Philip Benizi — whom the one he assaulted forgave and later welcomed into the order itself — made him, in the Servite tradition, an example of the conversion brought about by forgiveness offered without retaliation.
fontes: Archdiocese of São Paulo, 'São Peregrino: o padroeiro dos pacientes oncológicos'

itens.resumo: Italian Redemptorist lay brother (1726-1755), who died at the age of 29 and was canonized by Pius X in 1904; invoked as patron of expectant mothers, happy childbirths, children, and the falsely accused.
itens.corpo:
Gerard Majella was born in Muro Lucano, in Basilicata, on April 6, 1726, the son of a tailor. Orphaned of his father at the age of twelve, he grew up in extreme poverty and worked as a tailor's apprentice, later serving in the household of the bishop of Lacedonia. He tried to join the Capuchins but was turned away because of his frail health; only later was he received into the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, founded by Saint Alphonsus Liguori, where, having no education for the priesthood, he remained as a lay brother. He served as sacristan, gardener, porter, infirmarian, and tailor, joining this routine of manual labor to an intense life of prayer, penance, and charity. He died of tuberculosis at Materdomini, near Caposele (Campania), on October 16, 1755, at only 29 years of age.

The most delicate episode of his life occurred in 1754: a pregnant young woman, Neria Caggiano, falsely accused him of being the father of the child she was expecting. Gerard did not defend himself, withdrawing in silence to prayer; the woman later retracted her accusation and exonerated him. For this reason he is also invoked as patron of the falsely accused. His fame for holiness, however, was established above all around difficult childbirths. According to the tradition recorded in his process, months before he died he dropped a handkerchief at the home of the Pirofalo family; when one of the daughters ran to return it, he told her to keep it, since she might need it someday. Years later, now married and at death's door during childbirth, the woman asked for the handkerchief to be brought to her: the pains ceased and she gave birth to a healthy child. The acts of the process attest that he was called "il santo dei felici parti", the saint of happy childbirths, at a time when one in every three pregnancies did not come to term.

To other accounts attributed to his intercession are added episodes narrated in the canonization process: he is said to have walked on water to guide a boat of fishermen to shore during a storm, multiplied loaves of bread for the poor, blessed a farmer's harvest to free it from rats, and even revived a boy given up for dead after a fall. The testimonies gathered during the cause also describe phenomena of bilocation, levitation, and reading of consciences — elements that, without being the object of doctrinal definition, fed popular devotion and explain why the canonization process was opened shortly after his death.

Gerard was beatified by Leo XIII on January 29, 1893, and canonized by Pius X on December 11, 1904. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on October 16, and his main shrine is that of Materdomini, in Avellino. The Roman Martyrology lists him as a Redemptorist lay brother, and the Church presents him as a model of the holiness possible in non-priestly religious life, lived in the humblest services of the community. Besides expectant mothers and mothers, he is invoked by children (including those still in the womb), by maternity wards, for good confessions, by lay brothers, and by his native town, Muro Lucano.

itens.resumo: Seventeenth-century French religious sister to whom, according to tradition, Jesus revealed the devotion to the Sacred Heart.
itens.corpo: A Visitation nun at Paray-le-Monial, in France, Margaret Mary reported a series of apparitions of Jesus between 1673 and 1675, in which he is said to have entrusted to her the devotion to the Sacred Heart and asked for the institution of its own feast, now celebrated on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi. Her spiritual director, Claude de la Colombière, played a decisive role in spreading this devotion.

itens.resumo: Seventeenth-century French Jesuit, spiritual director of Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque and promoter of devotion to the Sacred Heart.
itens.corpo: As confessor of Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial, the Jesuit Claude de la Colombière recognized the authenticity of the revelations she reported about the Sacred Heart of Jesus and devoted himself to spreading this devotion, despite the initial skepticism of other religious. He later served as chaplain at the English court, a period during which he faced anti-Catholic persecution.

itens.resumo: Seventeenth-century Polish Jesuit, martyred with extreme cruelty by Cossack troops during the religious conflicts in Eastern Europe.
itens.corpo: A Jesuit devoted to preaching and to the reconciliation of Orthodox Christians with Rome in the region of present-day Belarus, Andrew Bobola was captured by Cossack troops in 1657, amid the religious and political wars that were shaking the region, and subjected to especially cruel torture and death before being canonized in 1938. He is co-patron of Poland.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Hubert Śmietanka — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5

itens.titulo: Saints Isaac Jogues and Companions (North American Martyrs)
itens.resumo: French Jesuit missionaries of the seventeenth century, martyred by Native peoples hostile to their mission among the Hurons and the Iroquois.
itens.corpo: A group of French Jesuits — among them Isaac Jogues, Jean de Brébeuf and others — devoted to the evangelization of the Huron and Iroquois peoples in the North American Great Lakes region, martyred between 1642 and 1649 in conflicts tied to the wars between rival Native nations and to the tensions of European colonization. They were canonized in 1930 as the "North American Martyrs."

itens.titulo: Saint Paul Miki and Companions (Martyrs of Japan)
itens.resumo: A group of 26 Christians — Japanese Jesuits, Franciscans and laypeople — crucified in Nagasaki in 1597 during the persecution of Christianity in Japan.
itens.corpo: In 1597, the Japanese ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered the arrest and execution of 26 Christians — among them the Japanese Jesuit Paul Miki, European Franciscans and Japanese laypeople, including teenagers — crucified on a hill in Nagasaki as part of the growing persecution of Christianity in Japan during that period. The group was canonized in 1862 and is venerated as the "26 Martyrs of Japan".
itens.imagem_credito: Foto: Photo: Andreas Praefcke — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0

itens.titulo: Saint Andrew Kim and Companions (Martyrs of Korea)
itens.resumo: Andrew Kim Taegon, the first native Korean priest, and more than one hundred companions martyred in the persecutions of Catholicism in Korea in the nineteenth century.
itens.corpo: Andrew Kim Taegon became the first native Korean priest, ordained in Shanghai after years of formation abroad, at a time when Catholicism was forbidden in Korea. He returned secretly to the country to exercise his ministry and was executed in 1846, at the age of 25. He and more than one hundred other Korean martyrs — most of them lay people — from persecutions that took place between the end of the eighteenth century and the nineteenth century were canonized by John Paul II in Seoul in 1984.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Ethan Doyle White — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.titulo: Saint Charles Lwanga and Companions (Martyrs of Uganda)
itens.resumo: A group of young Christians from the court of the Kingdom of Buganda, executed between 1885 and 1887 for refusing to renounce the Christian faith.
itens.corpo: Charles Lwanga and other young pages at the court of King Mwanga II of Buganda (present-day Uganda) were executed — many of them burned alive — between 1885 and 1887, for refusing both to abandon Christianity and to yield to the king's demands that were incompatible with the faith they professed. They were canonized by Paul VI in 1964, the first saints canonized from modern sub-Saharan Africa.

itens.resumo: Lord Chancellor of England in the sixteenth century and author of "Utopia", executed by Henry VIII for refusing to recognize the king as head of the Church in England.
itens.corpo: A humanist, lawyer, and friend of Erasmus of Rotterdam, Thomas More became Lord Chancellor of England under Henry VIII, but he resigned from the office and later refused to take the oath recognizing the king as supreme head of the Church of England, breaking with Rome over Henry's divorce. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London and beheaded in 1535. He is the patron saint of politicians and statesmen, and was canonized in 1935.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Rochester in the sixteenth century, the only English bishop to refuse to recognize Henry VIII as head of the Church in England, executed in 1535.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Rochester and respected theologian, John Fisher was the only English bishop to publicly resist Henry VIII's break with Rome, refusing to recognize the king as supreme head of the English Church. He was executed a few weeks before his friend Thomas More, in 1535, and both were canonized together in 1935.

itens.resumo: Archbishop of Canterbury in the twelfth century, murdered in his own cathedral by knights of King Henry II of England.
itens.corpo: Chancellor and personal friend of King Henry II before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Becket broke with his former ally by defending, with unexpected firmness, the rights and jurisdiction of the Church before the English crown. He was murdered inside his own cathedral in 1170 by knights who took literally an exasperated remark of the king. He quickly became one of the most venerated saints of the English Middle Ages.

itens.resumo: German duchess of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, known for her intense dedication to charity and for founding monasteries and hospitals in Silesia.
itens.corpo: Duchess of Silesia (today part of Poland), married while still young to Duke Henry I, Hedwig devoted a large part of her life and resources to founding monasteries, hospitals and a leper hospital, as well as promoting education. After being widowed, she withdrew to live among the Cistercian nuns she had sponsored, without taking formal vows. She is the patroness of Silesia and of victims of family conflicts.

itens.resumo: An eighteenth-century French pilgrim who lived as a voluntary beggar, traveling on pilgrimage to shrines across Europe.
itens.corpo: After being turned away by several religious orders because of his frail health and reserved temperament, Benedict Joseph Labre began to live as a mendicant pilgrim, traveling on foot to the main shrines of Europe and, in his last years, sleeping in the ruins of the Colosseum in Rome. He died in 1783 and was immediately acclaimed as a saint by the Roman people who knew him.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: José Luiz — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

itens.resumo: Spanish Franciscan friar who lived as a lay brother, served the poor, and became the patron of Eucharistic congresses.
itens.corpo:
Paschal Baylon was born on May 16, 1540, in Torrehermosa, in the former Kingdom of Aragon, into a peasant family. From childhood he worked as a shepherd and sought to learn to read so that he could pray the Office of the Virgin Mary. The biographical tradition highlights his honesty, austerity, and care for the poor.

In 1564 he entered the Reformed Franciscans as a lay brother. He performed humble tasks, such as cook, gardener, porter, and almsgiver, refusing priestly ordination because he understood that his vocation was to serve as an unordained religious. His life was marked by prayer, penance, humility, and devotion to the Eucharist. During a journey through France, according to hagiographical sources, he defended the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist before a Calvinist preacher and was nearly killed by a mob.

Paschal died in Villarreal, Spain, on May 17, 1592. He was beatified by Paul V in 1618 and canonized by Alexander VIII in 1690. In 1897, Leo XIII proclaimed him patron of Eucharistic congresses and associations. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on May 17; iconography usually depicts him in the Franciscan habit with a monstrance.
